The Yangtze icefish Neosalanx taihuensis is a small, short-lived osmerid endemic to freshwater systems of eastern China. Field surveys indicate that this species reaches a maximum recorded total length of 9.8 centimeters [Li = 9.8 centimeters], making it one of the smaller members of the family. The adult body mass corresponding to this ultimate size, based on length-weight regressions from lake populations, is approximately 3.0 grams [Wwi = approximately 3.0 grams]. These values position the species at the lower end of the size spectrum among icefishes, a trait likely linked to its semelparous life-history strategy and rapid metabolic turnover in warm, productive habitats. The larval stage begins with emergence from the egg, and under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 16.9 °C [T = 16.9 °C], the time required from fertilisation to eclosion is 11.0 days [ab = 11.0 days]. This brief incubation period is consistent with the pattern observed in other temperate osmerids and reflects the elevated developmental rates afforded by relatively warm incubation temperatures.

Sexual maturation in N. taihuensis occurs well before the attainment of maximum body size. Puberty is reached at a total length of 6.3 centimeters [Lp = 6.3 centimeters], a threshold corresponding to approximately two-thirds of the ultimate length. At this stage of gonad activation, the average wet weight of an individual is 0.73 grams [Wwp = 0.73 grams]. This relatively modest mass at maturity is typical of small-bodied, fast-growing fish that channel energy into early reproduction. The onset of vitellogenesis and spermiation is marked by rapid gonadal recrudescence, which in many teleosts is triggered by photoperiod and thermal cues. Following the attainment of sexual maturity, adults prepare for a single, highly synchronised spawning event. The total fecundity for a female during this singular reproductive bout, when held at a stable water temperature of 16.9 °C [T = 16.9 °C], has been recorded at 1,250 eggs .

The reproductive investment of Neosalanx taihuensis is tightly coupled with its abbreviated life history. A female produces approximately 1,250 eggs  over her lifetime, a total fecundity that reflects the trade-off between egg size and number at a temperature of 16.9 °C [T = 16.9 °C]. Each fertilised ovum is minute, and the wet weight at birth of a newly hatched prolarva, based on egg diameter data for the related species Osmerus mordax, is estimated at 0.00022 grams [Wwb = 0.00022 grams]. This exceedingly small neonatal mass, characteristic of pelagic spawning fish, necessitates a brief period of endotrophic nutrition from the yolk sac before the onset of exogenous feeding. The species typically completes its entire life cycle in a single year, with the maximum lifespan recorded at 365 days [am = 365 days] when reared at a constant 16.9 °C [T = 16.9 °C]. This annual life cycle, culminating in post-spawning mortality, is a classic example of obligate semelparity.

Life-history theory predicts that organisms with a high intrinsic mortality rate will evolve rapid development and early reproduction, a pattern clearly exemplified by N. taihuensis. At the population level, the species experiences high natural mortality following its single annual spawning event, with senescent adults dying after gamete release. The larval phase is brief, and under the thermal conditions of 16.9 °C [T = 16.9 °C], the age at hatch is 11.0 days [ab = 11.0 days], after which the yolk-sac larva quickly absorbs its endogenous reserves. The post-hatching growth trajectory is steep, driven by abundant zooplankton prey in the shallow lacustrine habitats the icefish occupies. The rapid attainment of puberty at 6.3 centimeters [Lp = 6.3 centimeters] total length and the corresponding wet weight of 0.73 grams [Wwp = 0.73 grams] highlights a strategy where somatic growth is truncated in favor of early allocation of resources to gamete production, a classic correlate of r-selected life histories.

Comparative data across the genus Neosalanx reveal that N. taihuensis occupies an intermediate position with respect to body size, with a maximum total length of 9.8 centimeters [Li = 9.8 centimeters] falling between its smaller congener N. anderssoni and the larger N. oligodontis. The ultimate wet weight of 3.0 grams [Wwi = 3.0 grams] is consistent with the allometric scaling relationships derived for the genus. Fecundity is correspondingly moderate; the single reproductive event yields 1,250 eggs per spawning [N_R_i = 1,250 eggs per spawning] at 16.9 °C [T = 16.9 °C], a value that aligns with both the body size and the annual life cycle of the species. The maximum lifespan of 365 days [am = 365 days] underscores its status as an annual fish, a strategy that is relatively uncommon among temperate freshwater teleosts but appears repeatedly in productive, unstable environments where high juvenile survival compensates for obligate adult death at a temperature of 16.9 °C [T = 16.9 °C]. This combination of rapid maturation, high fecundity, and short lifespan defines the species' ecological role as a fast-growing, capital-poor forager in the Yangtze River basin.
